questions: What are the two rectangles that make the L, and what is each area?
Why do we split the shape before measuring it?
segments.say: Two rectangles make one L. Show the L pulling apart into part A, 200 by 120, and part B, 120 by 140, then joining again: the areas are 24 000 and 16 800. Keep your student notes open at the area and composite shape definitions for this scene.

questions: Which edges are the inner steps of the L?
What is the perimeter if we add 200 + 120 + 80 + 140 + 120 + 260?
segments.say: Trace the edge for the perimeter. Follow the arrow around all six edges - 200, 120, 80, 140, 120 and 260 - for a perimeter of 920, and stress the two inner steps. Now try the perimeter questions on the worksheet in pairs.

questions: The box is 200 by 260, so why is 52 000 not the area?
Which part of the box is not part of the L?
segments.say: Watch out: the missing corner has no area. Show the 200 by 260 box around the L and point at its empty corner: the box overcounts, and the real area is 24 000 + 16 800 = 40 800.

questions: How do you find the area of any composite shape?
How is finding the perimeter different from finding the area?
segments.say: The takeaway. Land the summary: add the areas of the parts, and walk every side for the perimeter. Finish by taking the exit ticket on your own - its first question revisits exactly this box trap.
segments.watchFor: The area of the L-shape is the length times the width of its bounding box. Listen and look for it in pair talk and on the worksheet: any answer of 52 000 shows the trap - send them back to scene s3 and to the correct turn: The empty corner of the L was never filled, so it adds no area; count only what is there.
